name: FastPFor (SIMD-FastPFOR, SIMD-BP128)
baseline: Simple-8b and VByte (varint); also scalar FastPFOR/SimplePFOR
workload: Decoding sorted/small 32-bit integer lists (posting lists, delta coded) in blocks of 128+ integers with SSE SIMD, measured in billions of integers per second.
claimed_speedup: Paper (as quoted in search-result snippets, not opened): SIMD-FastPFOR within 10% of Simple-8b compression ratio while about 2x faster to decode; SIMD-BP128 more than 3x faster to decode than Simple-8b; SIMD schemes 2-3x faster than scalar FastPFOR and varint. README: decompresses at least 4 billion compressed integers per second (about 15 GB/s) on most x64 desktop/laptop processors, significantly faster than gzip, LZO, Snappy, LZ4.
stars_or_usage: 978 stars; used in zsearch, GMAP/GSNAP; Lucene 4.6 format referenced; ports to Java, C#, Go
tradeoffs: SIMD codecs need SSE2/SSSE3 (ARM64 NEON supported); best throughput on 128-integer blocks of 32-bit values; SIMD-FastPFOR trades some speed for 5-15% better ratio than SIMD-BP128; varint-G8IU in the library is patented.
caveats: Evidence tier B rests on the peer-reviewed paper 'Decoding billions of integers per second through vectorization' (Software: Practice and Experience 2015, arXiv 1209.2137); arXiv and Wiley were blocked in this environment, so the paper numbers are from WebSearch snippets only and the paper's CPU/compiler were not verified. The README states throughput but no head-to-head table against Simple-8b. This is the category's incumbent library named in the baseline list; entry is the paper-backed record for the SIMD schemes. GitHub redirects to the fast-pack org (fast-pack/FastPFOR). Independent competitor numbers: TurboPFor README lists FP_SimdFastPFor 8,748 MB/s decode vs Simple-8b 3,832 MB/s on ZIPF 100M (2019.11 table).
found_via: WebSearch: 'integer compression posting list SIMD bit packing faster than FastPFor SIMD-BP128 github'; opened github.com/lemire/FastPFor

name: SIMDCompressionAndIntersection
workload: Compression and decoding of sorted 32-bit integer lists with differential coding (SIMD-BP128, S4-BP128, SIMD-FastPFOR) plus SIMD intersection of sorted lists.
claimed_speedup: Paper (WebSearch snippets only): SIMD-BP128 nearly twice as fast as the previously fastest schemes (varint-G8IU and PFOR) while saving up to 2 bits per integer; SIMD-BP128-D1-NI 38% faster than SIMD-FastPFOR; S4-BP128-D4 as little as 0.7 CPU cycles per decoded 32-bit integer; SIMD schemes 2-3x faster than FastPFOR and varint with comparable ratio. README: 15 GB/s decompression.
tradeoffs: Requires SSE2 (SSE4.1 for some schemes); includes patented varint-G8IU implementation (README warns); research code with a larger API than simdcomp.
caveats: Tier B relies on the peer-reviewed paper 'SIMD Compression and the Intersection of Sorted Integers' (Software: Practice and Experience, arXiv 1401.6399); paper pages were not opened (arXiv blocked), numbers are from search snippets. Repo README has no benchmark table; advanced benchmarking is in a subfolder not opened. Star count not read. GitHub redirects to fast-pack org.
found_via: WebSearch: 'integer compression posting list SIMD bit packing faster than FastPFor SIMD-BP128 github' (paper 1401.6399 snippets); opened github.com/lemire/SIMDCompressionAndIntersection README via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: simdcomp
workload: SIMD binary packing (SIMD-BP128 core) of blocks of 128 32-bit integers, with optional delta coding.
claimed_speedup: README: decodes at least 4 billion compressed integers per second (about 15 GB/s) on desktop/laptop processors; 0.3 cycles per integer on Skylake (8+ billion integers per second); 'significantly faster than generic codecs like gzip, LZO, Snappy or LZ4'. Related paper (snippet only): SIMD-BP128 more than 3x faster to decode than Simple-8b.
stars_or_usage: 538 stars; used by upscaledb, EventQL, ManticoreSearch
tradeoffs: Blocks of exactly 128 integers; 32-bit values only; SSE/AVX and NEON backends; a Rust port exists (quickwit-oss/bitpacking).
caveats: README compares to gzip/LZO/Snappy/LZ4 only in words and gives cycles-per-integer without a head-to-head table against Simple-8b or varint; CPU for the 15 GB/s figure is not stated; paper-based comparison was not verified (arXiv blocked). Tier C for that reason. In the TurboPFor README (competitor-run) SC_SIMDPack128 decodes gov2.sorted at 9,488 MB/s vs Simple-8b 3,296 MB/s (2019.11 table, hardware not stated there). GitHub redirects to fast-pack/simdcomp.
found_via: WebSearch: 'AVX-512 integer compression bit packing library github faster than FastPFor simdcomp'; opened github.com/lemire/simdcomp

name: Stream VByte (streamvbyte)
workload: Byte-oriented 32-bit integer compression with a separated control stream; decoding from RAM to L1 of differentially coded real posting-list data sets.
claimed_speedup: Paper (WebSearch snippets only): decoding up to twice as fast as varint-G8IU on real data, more than 4 billion differentially coded integers per second on a 3.4 GHz Haswell, at times exceeding memcpy speed. README (no baseline): Apple M4 Max mixed 1-4 byte data encode ~27 GB/s, decode ~41 GB/s. TurboPFor issue #47 (competitor-run, Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz): StreamVByte docids decode 14,101.75 MB/s vs FastPFor 7,616.66 MB/s and MaskedVByte 6,507.48 MB/s.
stars_or_usage: 419 stars; ported to Rust, Go, Java and others
tradeoffs: Worse compression than bit-packing schemes (byte granularity, e.g. 9-10 bits/int in TurboPFor tables); SSE4.1 or NEON for speed, scalar fallback.
caveats: Tier B from the peer-reviewed paper (Information Processing Letters 130, 2018); paper pages blocked, so claims are snippet-only. benchmark_url is the competitor TurboPFor issue, whose compiler/flags are not stated. TurboPFor README claims its TurboByte matches or beats StreamVByte on some data; different winners per data set. GitHub redirects to fast-pack org.
found_via: WebSearch: '"Stream VByte" OR "Masked VByte" OR "SIMD-BP128" faster integer decoding paper code github'; opened github.com/lemire/streamvbyte

name: Masked VByte (MaskedVByte)
workload: Decoding standard-format VByte (LEB128-style) streams of 32-bit integers with SSE4.1/NEON, optional delta coding.
claimed_speedup: Paper (WebSearch snippet only): Masked VByte can be three times faster than a conventional VByte decoder when data is sufficiently compressible. TurboPFor README table (ZIPF 100M, 2019.11, competitor-run): MaskedVByte decode 9,524 MB/s vs FP_VByte 4,268 MB/s and PC_Vbyte 4,208 MB/s (about 2.2x, derived from page data).
stars_or_usage: 131 stars; integrated into Lucene prototype by a third party (per README)
tradeoffs: Works on the unmodified VByte format (drop-in decoder, no new format) but decode speed is below Stream VByte and bit-packing; encoder is plain scalar.
caveats: Tier B relies on the peer-reviewed paper 'Vectorized VByte Decoding' (ISWAG 2015, arXiv 1503.07387), not opened (arXiv blocked). The repo README has no benchmark numbers. The TurboPFor table is run by a competitor with CPU and flags not stated next to the table.
found_via: WebSearch: '"Stream VByte" OR "Masked VByte" OR "SIMD-BP128"...'; opened github.com/fast-pack/MaskedVByte and its README via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: TurboPFor-Integer-Compression
workload: Single-thread compress/decompress of 100M Zipfian integers (block size 128/256) and gov2.sorted delta-coded docids, MB/s and bits per integer.
claimed_speedup: README table 2019.11 (ZIPF 100M): TurboPFor256 decode 10,950 MB/s vs FP_SimdFastPFor 8,748 MB/s and Simple-8b 3,832 MB/s, at 5.04 bits/int vs 5.88 and 7.67; TurboByte+TurboPack decode 12,408 MB/s, encode 17,298 MB/s vs FP_VByte 4,268 / 5,200 MB/s. gov2.sorted: TurboPFor256 decode 7,128 MB/s vs Simple-8b 3,296 MB/s and PC.OptPFD 2,144 MB/s at lower bits/int.
tradeoffs: GPL-2.0 (commercial license offered), so copyleft; large C codebase with many codecs; SSE/AVX2/NEON/Power9.
caveats: First-party benchmark; hardware and compiler for the README tables not stated at the table. Table is dated 2019.11 and codecs inside the table (FastPFor, Simple-8b) are older versions. The same author's issue #47 (Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz, gcc flags unstated) shows TurboPFor256 docid decode 13,045 MB/s vs SimdFastPFor 13,818 MB/s and StreamVByte 14,101 MB/s, i.e. not faster than SIMD-FastPFor there. Marketing claim '>20 billion integers/s SIMD bit packing' (search snippet) not verified. Commit date from the github.com commits page; README itself says last update 12 APR 2026.
found_via: WebSearch: 'AVX-512 integer compression bit packing library github ...' and 'faster than Simple8b'; opened repo, README and issue #47

name: upack (μpack)
baseline: Rust bitpacking crate (port of simdcomp); also compared in README prose to StreamVByte
workload: Decompress/compress 128-integer blocks of u32 with AVX512/AVX2/NEON, plain, delta and delta-1 variants, in billions of ints per second.
claimed_speedup: BENCHMARKS.md AVX512 Zen5 (AMD 9950x), x128 decompress: upack-base 10.07B int/s vs bitpacking-base 8.85B (1.14x, derived from page data); delta 8.81B vs 3.82B (2.3x, derived). AVX2 Zen3 (5900HX): 6.13B vs 5.88B base, 3.58B vs 3.26B delta. Hetzner CCX13 AVX2: 6.20B vs 5.87B base, 3.72B vs 2.85B delta.
tradeoffs: Variable-size output blocks (partial blocks can be truncated) for better ratio on short lists; u32/u16 only, u64 not supported; Rust crate with zero dependencies.
caveats: Loses to the bitpacking baseline on NEON: Apple M4 base decompress 6.45B vs 7.01B and delta 5.12B vs 5.70B; Hetzner CAX11 NEON 2.46B vs 3.05B. Rust compiler version and flags not stated in README or BENCHMARKS.md as read; only CPU names. Does not compare against FastPFor, Simple-8b or varint, so baseline is off-list. Not a C++ library (Rust); no C API checked.
found_via: WebSearch: 'AVX-512 integer compression bit packing library github "faster than" FastPFor simdcomp'; opened github.com/lnx-search/upack, README and BENCHMARKS.md

name: varint-simd
baseline: prost varint, integer-encoding-rs and rustc LEB128 (scalar varint)
workload: Encoding and decoding sequences of random LEB128 varints bounded by each integer width (u8 to u64), millions of integers per second.
claimed_speedup: Coffee Lake i7-8850H, u32 decode: varint-simd unsafe 482.95 M int/s vs prost 196.05, rustc 191.37, integer-encoding-rs 120.16; u32 encode: 360.87 vs prost 77.402 (4.7x, derived from page data), rustc 157.95, integer-encoding-rs 125.00. u64 encode 303.72 vs prost 46.456 (6.5x, derived). Ryzen 5 2600X u32 decode 293.88 vs prost 150.05.
tradeoffs: Needs target-cpu set to a CPU with SSSE3/SSE4.1 (README says project will not compile otherwise); optional BMI2/AVX2/POPCNT/LZCNT paths; 'unsafe' variant requires padded input; Rust, not C++.
caveats: Benchmark source (benches/varint_bench.rs) and CPUs are public and README states native optimizations are used (target-cpu via .cargo/config.toml), but rustc version is not stated and the baselines are Rust libraries, not C++ varint. Tier A given with that gap; a verifier may lower it to C. This is single-integer varint, not block bit-packing.
found_via: WebSearch: 'varint-simd Rust SIMD varint encode decode faster than prost integer-encoding benchmark github'; opened README via raw.githubusercontent.com and github.com commits

name: ds2i (Partitioned Elias-Fano and OptPFor indexes)
baseline: OptPFD (OptPFor), Interpolative coding, Varint-G8IU, SIMD-BP128 era codecs
workload: Query processing time and index size on compressed inverted indexes (Gov2/ClueWeb09-style collections) for Elias-Fano, partitioned Elias-Fano, OptPFD and Interpolative.
claimed_speedup: Paper (WebSearch snippets only): partitioned Elias-Fano indexes are both faster and smaller than OptPFD, significantly faster than Interpolative, and slightly slower but significantly smaller than Varint-G8IU. No numbers read.
tradeoffs: Elias-Fano family needs sorted (monotone) sequences, not generic bit-packing; Boost dependency; research code; the experiments repo ot/partitioned_elias_fano is archived-for-history and now part of ds2i.
caveats: Tier B based on peer-reviewed papers (SIGIR 2014 Partitioned Elias-Fano Indexes; WSDM 2015), whose pages were not opened. Speed claim is index query time, not raw decode throughput. The baselines are not FastPFor/Simple-8b/varint directly. Last commit date from github.com commits page.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Elias-Fano partitioned inverted index compression github faster than SIMD-BP128 OptPFor'; opened github.com/ot/ds2i and ot/partitioned_elias_fano

name: opt_vbyte
workload: Inverted index compressed with VByte vs uniform / eps-optimal / optimal partitioning; space in bits per integer, index build time and query time.
claimed_speedup: README table: VByte docs 10.498 bpi, freqs 8.031 bpi, query 4.316 microseconds; VByte optimal partitioning docs 7.388 bpi, freqs 4.268 bpi, query 4.378 microseconds. So about 30-47% smaller at equal query time; not faster.
tradeoffs: Partitioning step adds build time and requires sorted lists; decode speed equal to VByte, no speedup.
caveats: Claim is compression ratio at the same speed, not a speed win (paper per search snippet says up to 2x better compression with fast decoding). Tier B from the peer-reviewed TKDE 2020 paper (arXiv 1804.10949, not opened); README table has no CPU or compiler. Included to document the varint-improving research.
found_via: WebSearch: '"On Optimally Partitioning Variable-Byte Codes" Pibiri Venturini github code'; opened github.com/jermp/opt_vbyte

name: VTEnc
workload: Compression ratio and encode/decode speed on sorted lists: ts.txt timestamps and gov2.sorted 32-bit docid lists, Core i7-6700HQ laptop.
claimed_speedup: ts.txt: VTEnc/1 decode 7.32 G/s vs Delta+FastPFor128 3.88 G/s, Delta+FastPFor256 3.61 G/s, Delta+VariableByte 3.43 G/s; ratio 26,622 vs 250.2 for FastPFor128. gov2.sorted: VTEnc/1 ratio 8.29 vs Delta+FastPFor128 6.21, but decode 210.99 M/s vs 615.64 M/s (slower).
tradeoffs: Targets sorted unsigned lists (8/16/32/64-bit); wins on compression ratio and on clustered data like timestamps, loses decode speed on gov2 docids; README warns format may change between versions.
caveats: Shootout is run by the VTEnc author in a separate repo (vteromero/integer-compression-benchmarks, 5 stars) on one laptop CPU (Core i7-6700HQ, Ubuntu 21.10); compiler flags not stated. Speed is mixed: faster than FastPFor only on the timestamp set. Pre-1.0 and unmaintained.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github integer compression library sorted integers SIMD delta faster than SIMDCompressionAndIntersection...'; opened github.com/vteromero/integer-compression-benchmarks and VTEnc
